gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much power any of the candidate NASes uses when it runs around the clock. Dong Knows Tech measured the Synology DS225+ at about 275 Wh per 24 hours with two hard drives, which works out to an average of about 11.5 W and roughly 100 kWh a year.
standout_why: ChatGPT cited only Synology's Drive Technical Specifications pages (synology.com/en-us and en-global /dsm/7.4/software_spec/synology_drive). I opened the en-us page: it lists software limits only (32 versions per file, 500,000 files per client, 64 sync tasks, OS minimums) and contains no figures for power, noise, throughput or sync speed on any model. The other results (KB help pages, release notes, the 2020 Drive white paper, patchletter) are about software. ChatGPT's answer does tell the shopper they will be 'responsible for uptime', but it never says what a NAS that is always on draws or costs to run. No rival page in the results has a measurement from a named reviewer.
decides: This supports the DS225+ as the pick, because a freelancer's NAS replacing Dropbox stays on 24/7. Dong Knows measured it at about 11.5 W on average with two HDDs. LinuxLinks measured the Asustor AS5402T at 29.2 W in operation with its disks idle (2× 7200 rpm HDD plus 2× NVMe). QNAP lists the TS-264 at 29.086 W typical with all bays filled. Those two are roughly 2.5 times the DS225+, but the test conditions are not the same. For the UGREEN DXP2800, igor'sLAB measured 5.6 W standby and 14.5 W during transfers with only an NVMe SSD and no HDDs, and OCinside measured about 7 W idle without naming the drives. Neither figure can be compared directly with Dong Knows' two-HDD number. Running cost does not change the pick away from Synology. It does give the page a sourced running-cost line that no rival has.

findings.label: Measured energy use per 24 hours
findings.source_title: Synology DS225+ Review (vs. DS224+): A Solid Upgrade to 2.5GbE Connectivity — Dong Ngo, Dong Knows Tech (full review 2025-08-04)
findings.note: Measured by Dong Ngo with two hard drives installed. 275 Wh ÷ 24 h = 11.46 W. 275 Wh × 365 = 100.4 kWh a year. Ngo reports the noise as only 'a subtle hum, audible only in a quiet room', with no dB figure.

findings.label: Network transfer (reviewer's statement)
findings.value: Real-world rates matched the 2.5 Gbps port (no MB/s figure in the text)
findings.source_title: Synology DS225+ Review (vs. DS224+) — Dong Knows Tech
findings.note: The read/write charts are images, and the article text gives no number. Treat this as a qualitative statement from a named reviewer.

findings.label: Noise at idle (NASCompares)
findings.source_title: Synology DS225+ NAS Review – Rob Andrews, NASCompares (posted 2025-08-04)
findings.note: The article does not give the measurement distance or the drives used. NASCompares' power figures in the same article (16.98 W access, 6.08 W HDD hibernation) are identical to Synology's spec figures, so this noise number may also be a spec value rather than NASCompares' own measurement. Use it with that caveat.

findings.label: Measured wall power (igor'sLAB)
findings.value: 0.6 W off/WoL, 5.6 W standby, 14.5 W during data transfer
findings.source_title: Ugreen NASync DXP2800 NAS im Test – Tim Kutzner, igor'sLAB (2024-05-08, updated 2025-05-31)
findings.note: Measured at the wall with only one NVMe SSD installed and all HDDs removed, so with two HDDs fitted the draw would be higher. The 10 GB file transfer reached the 2.5GbE limit according to the text; the numbers are in charts only.

findings.label: Measured noise (igor'sLAB)
findings.value: 33.2 dB(A) idle, 35.6 dB(A) load, at 40 cm
findings.source_title: Ugreen NASync DXP2800 NAS im Test – igor'sLAB
findings.note: Voltcraft SL-200 meter at 40 cm, Lo mode, 125 ms. The room reading is also listed as 33.2 dB(A), so the idle reading did not rise above the room's background level. Only an NVMe SSD was installed, with no HDDs.

findings.label: Measured power and RAID 1 write (OCinside)
findings.value: ≈7 W idle, 34.7 W max under stress; ≈181 MB/s writing a 50 GB file to RAID 1
findings.source_title: Ugreen DXP2800 NAS Review, page 4 – OCinside
findings.note: The 34.7 W maximum came from a combined CPU, RAM and disk stress test. The page does not name the drives. The 50 GB write took 290 s, which is about 176–181 MB/s. iperf3 averaged 950 Mbit/s, but the test network was capped at 1 GbE. The page shows no date or author.

findings.label: Measured wall power (LinuxLinks)
findings.value: 29.2 W in operation with disks idle, 15.4 W disks hibernating, 36.8 W copying 9 GB HDD-to-HDD, 0.6 W S3 sleep
findings.source_title: Asustor Nimbustor 2 Gen2 AS5402T Review, page 4 – Steve Emms, LinuxLinks (2024-03-18)
findings.note: Measured with 2× 6TB 7200 rpm HDD and 2× NVMe SSD, EuP disabled, WOL and WOW enabled. 29.2 W × 24 h = 0.70 kWh a day, about 2.5 times Dong Knows' DS225+ figure, but with faster drives and two SSDs.

findings.label: Maker's rated power (not an independent measurement)
findings.note: QNAP's own figure, 'tested with drives fully populated' (2 bays), with no drive models named. Listed here only for context next to the independent figures. The spec page gives no noise figure.
